planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable; Cascade Creeper spreads readily by stolons to form a dense groundcover, useful for covering shaded ground quickly.

directions: Tuck divisions into moist, well-drained woodland soil enriched with compost, and water regularly the first season while the spreading stolons take hold. Cascade Creeper is a vigorous, fast-spreading foamflower selection bred to knit together into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover more quickly than clump-forming Tiarella cultivars, with lobed, maple-like green leaves that take on burgundy tones in cooler weather. Fluffy spikes of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage in spring, drawing early pollinators to the shade garden. Because of its spreading habit, it is especially useful for covering a shaded slope, filling in under trees, or edging a woodland path, though it is more assertive than compact clumping Tiarella selections and needs more room to roam. Established plantings tolerate some dry shade once rooted in, though consistent moisture keeps the groundcover densest and most attractive.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Fern and Foamflower Selection for Shade Gardens

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable; Neon Lights has unusually bright chartreuse-gold foliage that lights up a dim shaded spot.

directions: Tuck divisions into moist, well-drained woodland soil enriched with compost, and water regularly the first season while the plant establishes. Neon Lights is a foamflower selection grown chiefly for its unusually bright chartreuse-gold, deeply lobed foliage, which glows in a dim, shaded corner far more vividly than the muted greens typical of most Tiarella cultivars, with fine dark veining adding contrast against the bright leaf color. Fluffy spikes of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage in spring, adding a soft textural accent to the bold leaf display. The vivid color makes it an especially effective companion to dark-leaved heucheras, hostas, or hellebores, where the contrast draws the eye through a shaded border. Consistent moisture keeps the foliage from scorching, and dividing congested clumps every few years in spring keeps the planting vigorous.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Fern and Foamflower Selection for Shade Gardens

common_name: Crow Feather Tiarella (Deeply Cut Dark-Centered Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable; Crow Feather has finely dissected, feathery leaves marked with a dark central blotch.

directions: Tuck divisions into moist, well-drained woodland soil enriched with compost, and water regularly the first season while the plant establishes. Crow Feather is a foamflower selection with finely dissected, deeply cut, almost fern-like leaves marked by a dark blackish-purple central blotch that fades outward into green, giving the foliage a striking feathered pattern that stands out among the broader, less-divided leaves of many other Tiarella cultivars. Fluffy spikes of white to pale pink star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage in spring, adding a light textural accent to the intricately patterned leaves below. The fine, lacy leaf texture pairs beautifully with bolder hostas and heucheras in a mixed shade border. Consistent moisture keeps the foliage looking its best, and dividing congested clumps every few years in spring maintains vigor.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Fern and Foamflower Selection for Shade Gardens

common_name: Sea Foam Tiarella (Finely Cut Lacy Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable; Sea Foam has finely cut, lacy green foliage and produces an especially heavy flush of frothy white flower spikes in spring.

directions: Tuck divisions into moist, well-drained woodland soil enriched with compost, and water regularly the first season while the plant establishes. Sea Foam is a foamflower selection with finely cut, lacy, deep green foliage and an especially heavy spring flush of frothy, bottlebrush-like white flower spikes that live up to the plant's common name, foamflower, more vividly than many other Tiarella cultivars. The lacy leaf texture provides fine-grained contrast against bolder hostas, heucheras, and ferns in a shaded border, and the foliage remains attractive through the growing season after the spring bloom fades. Consistent moisture keeps the delicate-looking foliage from scorching, though established plantings tolerate some dry shade once well rooted. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and encourage the heaviest flowering.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Fern and Foamflower Selection for Shade Gardens
